title: Waris Shah, who lit up Punjab
titleOriginal: پیر سید وارث شاہ رحمۃ اللہ علیہ
takeaway: Great poetry keeps giving light for centuries.
scene: A tribute to Waris Shah, the 18th-century Punjabi poet who wrote 'Heer', the most famous love story in Punjab. Almost every Punjabi poet looks up to him, and Dr. Ahmad is no exception.

original: چانن تیری سخن وری دا پھیلیا چار چوفیرے
ایسی شمع جلائی وارثؒ ہو گئے دور ہنیرے
transliteration: Chaanan teri sukhan-vari da phailiya chaar chufere
Aisi shamaa jalaai Waris, ho gaye door hanere
translation: The light of your poetry has spread in every direction;
Waris, you lit such a candle that the darkness went away.
couplets.story: Waris Shah's poetry spread light everywhere. It was like a candle so bright that it chased the darkness away.

original: سگھڑ سیانے ایس کان چوں جھولیاں نے بھر لیندے
ہیر دے قصے اندر وارثؒ ہیرے ہین بکھیرے
transliteration: Sughar siyaane is kaan chon jholiyaan ne bhar lainde
Heer de qisse andar Waris heere hain bakhere
translation: Wise and skilled people fill their laps from this mine:
Waris scattered diamonds all through the story of Heer.
couplets.story: His book 'Heer' is like a mine full of diamonds. Clever people keep finding treasures in it and filling their pockets.

original: لوکاں دی نبضاں نوں ٹوہ کے ایسے شعر بنائے
سدا لئی نے جھلدے رہنے وارثؒ شاہ پھریرے
transliteration: Lokaan di nabzaan nu toh ke aise shair banaaye
Sada layi ne jhulde rehne Waris Shah phareere
translation: He felt people's pulse and wrote verses to match;
Waris Shah's flags will keep flying forever.
couplets.story: He understood ordinary people so well, like a doctor feeling their pulse, that he wrote exactly what they felt. His fame will fly like a flag forever.

original: بن پراں توں اڈ اڈ پہنچن عاشق وچ جھنگ سیالے
جس تھاویں محبوب دلاں دے وارثؒ لائے ڈیرے
transliteration: Bin paraan ton ud ud pohnchan aashiq vich Jhang Siyaale
Jis thaaveen mehboob dilaan de Waris laaye dere
translation: Without wings, lovers fly all the way to Jhang of the Sials,
the place where Waris, beloved of hearts, set up camp.
couplets.story: Lovers 'fly' without wings to Jhang, Heer's homeland, because that's where Waris Shah's story lives.

original: علموں عقلوں حسبوں نسبوں لا ثانی لا فانی
توں سوچاں دا وارث اچا تیرے گیان اچیرے
transliteration: Ilmon aqlon hasbon nasbon laa-saani laa-faani
Toon sochaan da Waris uchcha, tere giaan uchere
translation: In learning, wisdom and noble lineage, matchless and undying:
you are the lofty heir (waris) of thought, and your wisdom is lofty.
couplets.story: In knowledge, wisdom and family, Waris Shah has no equal, and he'll never be forgotten. The poet plays on his name: 'waris' means 'heir', and he truly is the heir of great thinking.

original: تیرے قلم سوچیرے بخشی ایسی تڑپ دلاں نوں
جدوں وی پڑھیئے ہیر تیری نوں لگن زخم گھنیرے
transliteration: Tere qalam sochere bakhshi aisi tarap dilaan nu
Jadon vi parhiye Heer teri nu, lagan zakhm ghanere
translation: Your thoughtful pen gave hearts such longing
that whenever we read your 'Heer', it opens deep wounds.
couplets.story: His pen filled hearts with such strong longing that every time you read 'Heer', it hurts in the deepest way.

original: کھول کے کھنب خیالاں والے اڈاں وچ ہواواں
نظر کرم اوہدی توں احمدؔ جاگن بھاگ وی میرے
transliteration: Khol ke khamb khayaalaan vaale udaan vich havaavaan
Nazar-e-karam ohdi ton Ahmad jaagan bhaag vi mere
translation: I spread the wings of my imagination and fly through the air;
Ahmad, by his kind glance, my own fortune awakens too.
couplets.story: Inspired by Waris Shah, the poet's imagination spreads its wings and flies. He feels that Waris Shah's blessing has woken up his own luck as a poet.

deeper: Waris Shah's 'Heer' is read by Sufis as an allegory. Heer is the soul, Ranjha is the seeker (or the Divine), and the struggle to be together is the soul's journey to God. Dr. Ahmad's many images of Heer, Ranjha and the jogi's earrings all go back to this book. Asking for Waris Shah's 'kind glance' (nazar-e-karam) treats him as a saint whose blessing helps.
why: It introduces Waris Shah, whose 'Heer' is the key to understanding most of the love imagery in this book.
prompt: Is there a story or book that has stayed with you and shaped how you see things?
